question: Why does the Beets lane reproduce badly (31.3% spread at n=3) while Fastify reproduces to 1.7%?

inputs.per_task_method: Codex reports cumulative thread totals; a task's cost is its final usage snapshot minus the previous task's.

finding: Beets does not vary because one task is unstable. Per-task variability is comparable in both lanes; what differs is whether it cancels. In Fastify the per-task deviations offset (cancellation ratio 12.4x) and no replicate is consistently dear. In Beets they align (ratio 1.1x): one replicate is the most expensive in 6 of 7 tasks and another the cheapest in 6 of 7, so deviations compound instead of averaging out.
mechanism: The workflow is one persistent session, so context accumulates across tasks and roughly two thirds of weighted cost is cached input. A session that pulls in more context early carries that penalty into every later task. Fastify re-converges -- its cheapest first task, r2 at 87,056 against 152,573, still ends with the largest final context -- so early exploration is traded against later exploration and final context lands within 5%. Beets never re-converges: final context spreads 40%.
not_supported: Cache warming across runs: the cached share of input is flat at 95.5-97.3% across all six sessions.
A single pathological task: the spread is distributed, with task-07 contributing 35%, task-05 21% and task-06 20%.
Task file overlap: both lanes change exactly one distinct production file per task.
consequence: At three replicates the Beets lane cannot resolve a treatment effect below roughly 30%. Fastify at 1.7% can resolve far smaller effects. Adding Beets replicates narrows the median but does not remove the compounding, because the correlation is within a session rather than between sessions.
